items.title: Notion’s Founder on the One Thing Your AI Is Missing
items.content: Everybody can start making their own software, no? In some sense, the original vision of the 60s, 70s, hippie generation of computing come to life, and that's actually why Notion was started. Notion was about how do we bring this computing power to as many people as possible without forcing them to learn how to code. Hello and welcome to the Every Podcast. I'm Dan Shipper. And I'm Natalia Quintero. And this week we're talking about a conversation that you had, Dan, with Ivan Zhao, CEO and founder of Notion. Can you tell me a little bit about what you learned? Yeah, it was such an interesting conversation because Notion is the original, one of the original no code companies. The way it's structured with databases and forms and blocks, it's all designed to allow you to build something that looks kind of like software without knowing how to code. But AI like totally changed that. Now anyone can Vibe code whatever they want. You don't really need a block system. You don't really need the whole Notion interface in order to make something that looks like software. And so it kind of forced them to reinvent what they are and reinvent or rethink the original vision for their product. I've been a user of Notion for a long time, and the product has evolved quite a bit. What do you think makes Ivan the right leader to lead this transformation? You know him well. Ivan is one of those interesting people. I think there's some kind of soul overlap between Notion and Every, and I think that comes from who Ivan is as a person. You know, the way that he dresses and the way that they furnish their office, and there's so much attention to detail and so much craft in what they do. And I think that that's actually sorely missing from the... pantheon of AI CEOs. Like when you really think about what kinds of CEOs are around in this era, there are very few people who care a lot about the details and the feeling of work and what you make. And especially in a world where everyone's afraid of AI taking jobs and how do you keep the work that we do feeling human or feeling special. I think that there's something really interesting happening with Notion and Ivan is the right person to make that happen. So if you didn't catch it at thesis, let's turn over now to a conversation between Dan Shipper and Ivan Zao from Notion. Welcome, really excited to have you here. Good to be here. And thank you for sponsoring this, for making this event possible. I didn't know until I got here. Yeah, Ivan asked me backstage, he was like, how much was this? And I was like, I don't know, but next time, we'll make it bigger if you want to pay a little more. It's big enough. Good love. Great. Nice to be here. So in addition to sponsoring this conference, you make Notion. And I think of you as, we were talking about this a little bit backstage. I think there is a spiritual similarity between the way that Notion and every think about work. And I think that comes from you specifically. you think a lot about the craft of work and thinking well with software. And I think when we are, like in AI there seems like there's this bifurcation between people who think it's all slop and people who think that you can actually do good work with it. And I'm curious like how you're thinking about this as you're bringing Notion into this era and in your own life. We're probably in the one year after the Vibe coding phase at this point, for most people. Probably in this room. A year ago, people say software is dead, Vibe code everything. Then nine months ago, people realized you need to maintain them. I'm actually in different directions. I love the spirit of Vibe coding. Actually, if anything, Vibe coding, the spirit is the spirit that YNOTION was started in the first place. I think so, right? Yeah. If I share this with you all, it's... When I was in school, last year college, I was inspired by early days of computing. People in the 60s and 70s, or even the 50s, their idea of a software, it's a me…

items.title: TokenEconomizer: Learning from Experience to Make AI Coding Agents More Efficient
items.content: At a glance Developers use AI coding agents in the same codebases day after day, yet agents often start each session from scratch: rediscovering familiar facts, loading unused tools, and repeating unsuccessful approaches. TokenEconomizer is an open-source plugin that learns from an agent’s past sessions in a repository to reduce waste in future sessions, without modifying the agent or its underlying model. Across 277 real bug-fixing tasks, TokenEconomizer reduced costs by 18.4–30.9% across multiple AI coding agents. Costs fell in every repository tested, while task success rates remained broadly stable. AI coding agents are increasingly helping developers fix bugs and build features largely on their own, but every interaction with their models consumes tokens. In each session , an agent sends instructions, tool descriptions, and session history to its model. Most efforts to reduce this cost focus on individual tasks. Yet developers return to the same repositories, giving agents an opportunity to learn from previous work. Without that learning, an agent may repeatedly rediscover how to run tests, load tools it never uses, or spend dozens of turns revisiting the same error.  In our paper, TokenEconomizer: Experience-Driven Black-Box Cost Control for Coding Agents , we ask a simple question: can experience in a repository help an agent solve future tasks more efficiently? TokenEconomizer, an open-source plugin from UC Berkeley, Microsoft Research, and Microsoft Security, turns completed sessions into guidance for subsequent ones. It reduces waste without changing the agent or its underlying model, so developers can use it alongside the coding agents they already rely on. Figure 1. Each finished session teaches TokenEconomizer something about the repository, so later sessions cost less tokens.   Where the tokens go We first profiled Claude Code on 60 tasks from SWE-Bench, a benchmark of real bug fixes in open-source Python projects, running each repository’s…

items.title: Import AI 481: AI sub-contractors; a wet lab for AI; and subterfuge during development
items.content: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now AI systems are getting good at sub-contracting to make themselves better: …AI can now productively spend money to improve itself… Researchers have developed FrontierML, a benchmark “that measures how well agents turn capital into model performance on challenging, end-to-end machine learning tasks.” It shows that today’s frontier systems are already able to, when given some money, turn this into improving their own performance on a basket of 21 distinct tasks. 21 long-horizon tasks “inspired by real work at frontier labs, neolabs, and academic institutions”. These tasks span six category areas, including LLM training, efficiency, vision & audio, computer use, applied NLP, and math & games. “Each task provides the agent with the same setup: a 12-hour CPU sandbox, a wallet with $10, $50, or $200, a few validation samples, and a task description.” Example task: Agents try to solve the tasks in pretty different ways. E.g, for one task about generating screenshots, the top-scoring agent fine-tuned a diffusion model using LoRA, while other high-scoring approaches involved an LLM writing a drawing program that is then rendered. Key features: Scaling spending : “Give agents $10, $50, and $200 per task to spend on training compute and data, and evaluate whether agents can use the additional capital productively,” they write. “In our experiments, we find that stronger agents are able to reliably improve their submissions with greater access to capital.” Open-ended & end-to-end : “In each task, agents can choose architectures, source data, implement training, provision compute, evaluate checkpoints, and optimize inference,” they write. items.title: [AINews] GPT-6.2 Astra, the #2 Frontier Model is better and 20%-600% cheaper, but has mixed reviews; 6.2 Sol likely main workhorse
items.content: OpenAI shipped GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol today, two days before Anthropic’s expected first trading day . In Artificial Analysis ’ tests, Sol ties September’s Astra at about 15% of the cost per task . New Astra scores 62 on the Intelligence Index, just behind Fable 5.2 at 65. Net net, Anthropic still owns the world’s best model, but OpenAI owns the world’s most efficient models in terms of intelligence per $. What’s more unusual about this launch is the STRONGLY negative influencer feedback… which prompted a defensive response … View post on X ↗ We think that some of this is overreacting and normal influencer tendency to either have everything be 🤯🤯🤯 or the literal WORST.MODEL.EVER, BUT also that some of the criticisms are valid, and the RL artefacts are noticeable and downright bizarre (don’t even get us started about the terrible launch video ). However, we still use it to automate our work and that’s all that matters in the end. items.title: Cloudflare Joins the Jevolution and Labels Itself a Neolab
items.content: Cloudflare has been one of the essential infrastructure companies of the web for the past decade and a half. But now, it’s turning into a neolab — at least according to a presentation at AI Engineer Code Summit by Michelle Chen , who runs Cloudflare’s AI Platform on the product side. We’ll get into what exactly a neolab is in a minute (the short version: they build models and they’re not called OpenAI or Anthropic). Cloudflare is claiming to be one because it too has begun to launch models. Two System One models , to be precise: Clef and Clairic. As Chen explained in her talk, Clef is a decision model directly inspired by TypeSafe AI’s revolutionary Jev model , while Clairic is a new type of system one model that Cloudflare calls an “extract” model . In an interview with Latent Space after her presentation, Chen hinted that Cloudflare won’t just be producing system one models. There will be large language models, too. “We're not being a neolab [to] only launch system one models, even though it makes sense for our infrastructure. We've kind of entered this Pandora's box now, right? We opened it, now the possibilities are endless.” Chen said it’s “not just system one models, but potentially reasoning models that we've been experimenting with, and other LLMs and whatnot.” However, she added that these probably won’t be pre-trained models built from scratch, like the frontier labs produce. “I don't think that's our focus, but I think we can take existing resources out there and make [them] a lot more efficient and effective.” She noted that “most of our team really just does post-training,” so that will be the focus in model development. What is a neolab and is Cloudflare really one? The term neolab literally means a ‘new lab’ and it was coined last November by Stephanie Palazzolo from The Information, who defined it as “a new generation of research-focused AI startups.” Deedy Das , a partner at Menlo Ventures and an AI influencer, runs a big list of neolabs . It inclu…

items.title: Building Visual Intelligence — Andreas Blattmann & Dustin Podell, Black Forest Labs
items.content: This episode is sponsored by Deepgram. Try Deepgram for voice agents that truly understand your context! #contextiseverything Not many people know that Stable Diffusion is why I went fulltime into AI (I aptly titled Multiverse, not Metaverse to call out Zuck’s mistaken investment). It turns out that Dustin Podell also had the same aha moment - quitting his day job when the model came out. But we took very different paths… I stuck to what I knew in human content creation, and Dustin immersed deep into AI content creation with Andreas Blattmann , co-inventor of Latent Diffusion and the rest of the world-leading imagegen crew at Stability AI. Stability fell apart, but Anj Midha helped the core group spin out to BFL, which immediately built an incredible new imagegen model in the Flux series. But why are they now going into video and world models? Andreas gives an example you can try with one hand. If somebody tosses you a ball, your hand starts moving before the ball reaches you. You can do that without being able to write down the trajectory. When he talks about building visual intelligence , that’s the kind of knowledge he means. A still can show you where the ball is. A video shows you how it got there. The sound of impact can tell you when it hit something, even if the camera missed the contact. That’s BFL’s argument for training FLUX 3 on the three signals together. BFL’s FLUX 3 release The horse in motion is one of the FLUX 3 examples we show in the intro. The audio examples are worth playing with the sound on. FLUX 3 Video What a moving camera teaches you Suppose the camera starts in front of a person and pans around them. At some point the model owes you the back of their head. Andreas thinks ordinary two-dimensional video contains a great deal of evidence about what objects look like from other angles. items.title: BIS Takes on Compute Leakage
items.content: A 132-page export control rule landed Monday morning, and the Commerce Department’s own press release credited Treasury and the NSC with writing it. Days after the Megaspeed scandal ended Jensen Huang’s run at Nvidia, Washington is moving to close the cloud loophole that, by ChinaTalk’s estimate, supplies two-fifths of China’s AI compute. Two Biden NSC alumni weigh in: ⁠Chris McGuire⁠ , now senior fellow for China and emerging technologies at the Council on Foreign Relations after a stint as deputy senior director for technology and national security, and ⁠Julian Gewirtz⁠ , the former senior director for China and Taiwan affairs now a senior research scholar at Columbia SIPA. We discuss… Three loopholes closed in 132 pages — license requirements for chips headed to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil; a cap on compute rented to Chinese firms; and a TSMC backdoor closed for the second time. The Northern Virginia problem — why a rule that stops at the US border could simply move China’s rented compute from Johor to the Washington suburbs. Who wrote the rule — what crediting Treasury and the NSC says about Commerce’s credibility, and whether Trump holds firm in Shenzhen. Does Xi know the numbers — whether Beijing escalates or doubles down on the bet that it can (again) talk Trump into loosening controls. Jensen’s soup vendor — the customer-concentration fear that pushed Nvidia toward Asian neoclouds and China. Zero consequences for three million chips — why export controls need their BNP Paribas moment, and what that has to do with AI safety. Listen now on your favorite podcast platform . An aerial shot of new data centers in the IBTEC district of the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone in Malaysia. items.title: MOFCOM's New Rules: Digging For Leverage
items.content: With the world scrambling to diffuse China’s rare earth weapon, Chinese regulators have apparently been tasked with identifying alternative sources of potential leverage. MOFCOM’s recent work created legal mechanisms to restrict the flow of a curious collection of products: tunnel boring machines, dredging components, solar manufacturing equipment, biotechnology, and drones. At first glance, this seems like an eclectic list, but these technologies are connected beyond the fact that they are all made in China. Today, we’re unpacking the geopolitical incentives that made them MOFCOM’s business. This is part two of our series on MOFCOM’s October 2026 regulatory drops. In part one, we analyzed the October 16th proposals for regulating AI technologies. Today’s installment tackles the October 16th proposals for biotech and solar and the mixed bag from October 19th. We explore: Why parsing China’s trade policy requires looking beyond the US-China rivalry to Beijing’s bilateral relations with other capitals — and why India in particular is under fire; How tunnel boring machines and dredgers help us understand China’s ambitions as a regional power; Beijing’s playbook for keeping foreign countries dependent on its solar provisions; And, what biotech and drones tell us about China’s approach to intellectual property. ChinaTalk is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support our work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber. items.title: Jensen Out, MATCH Act In?
items.content: Jordan Schneider, Dylan Patel, and Jordan Nanos of SemiAnalysis record an emergency pod after Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO. We discuss: Why Jensen’s exit could become cover for “really stupid laws” — and why Dylan backs the MATCH Act but thinks RASA is a mistake. The game theory of remote access: renting compute to Chinese firms as margin capture and a kill switch, versus closing the Malaysia loophole outright. “Flip the table”: why equipment controls beat chip and model controls, and how close Huawei’s silicon now is. Why no American lab has out-built Kimi or DeepSeek in open models. Nvidia without Jensen: talent retention, Rubin and Feynman execution risk, and who should run the company. Colette Kress’s exposure, Supermicro and Megaspeed, and a fight over whether this amounts to the “nationalization” of Nvidia. Listen now on your favorite podcast app .
